002e5577aa298cd4: Untuk seketika, perkataan ‘paling bodoh’ menjadi kata kunci yang masyhur. Ini ekoran seorang siswi Fakulti Ekonomi daripada Universiti Malaya (UM) bernama Ummi Umairah Bakhit menyelar tindakan segelintir Melayu yang menderma wang hasil titik peluh untuk membantu golongan elit disabitkan kes rasuah. Ummi menyatakan perbuatan tersebut adalah sesuatu yang paling bodoh selain tidak bermoral. Kenyataan, atau lebih tepat soalan Ummi tersebut dilontarkan ketika acara dalam sebuah forum terbuka yang menampilkan panel antara lain seorang DJ terkenal, Menteri Besar Johor Onn Hafiz Ghazi dan Menteri Besar Selangor Amirudin Shari. Forum itu adalah sebahagian daripada acara Sidang Kemuncak Pemimpin Muda Masa Depan Antarabangsa di Kuala Lumpur.

Dalam pertanyaan Ummi itu, beliau mempersoalkan tindakan sesetengah orang yang memilih menderma bagi membantu pesalah rasuah, Najib Razak, untuk membayar denda mahkamah berjumlah RM50 juta bagi membolehkan dirinya layak menjadi tahanan di rumah. Suis ketokohan Onn Hafiz nampak off atau terpadam seketika manakala DJ terkenal dalam forum tersebut nampaknya tersangkak, gugup lagi gagap untuk menjawab soalan yang tidak dijangka itu.

Bukan sahaja kata bodoh, sebetulnya Ummi mempertikaikan tindakan mempertahankan rasuah dan korupsi dengan menyebut-nyebut perihal skandal Tabung Haji dan lain-lain. Ini adalah intipati yang sepatutnya menjadi sorotan.

Meskipun berbahasa Inggeris, kata bodoh yang digunakan memang menular menjadi racun dalam pembuluh darah ramai penyokong Najib. Selepas keratan video itu menjadi tular, ramai dalam kalangan ahli Umno di media sosial ‘menghunus keris’ kepada siswi ini. Ada yang malah meminta Universiti Malaya mengambil tindakan terhadap beliau. Ummi malah diugut, diancam dan dinista. Padahal kata-kata Ummi menistai perbuatan rasuah itu adalah sesuatu yang terpuji.

Setelah ancaman terhadap Ummi menjadi-jadi, Menteri Pendidikan Tinggi Zambry Abdul Kadir akhirnya menegaskan mahasiswa mempunyai hak untuk bersuara dan tiada sebarang tindakan tatatertib akan dikenakan terhadapnya susulan pertanyaan kritis mengenai dana sumbangan Najib itu. Noor Azuan Abu Osman, naib canselor Universiti Malaya turut terpaksa tampil memberikan kenyataan rasmi yang senada.

Kenyataan kedua-dua tokoh besar dalam pengajian tinggi ini amat penting. Ini kerana bekas naib canselor Universiti Malaya antara tahun 1988 sehingga 1991, Syed Hussein Alatas iaitu seorang pemikir, yang karya masyhurnya bertajuk ‘Rasuah: Sifat, Sebab dan Fungsi’ pernah mempopularkan satu terma berkesan. Terma tersebut ialah gejala bebalisme. Ia datang daripada kata bebal, yang secara mudahnya bermaksud bodoh. Malah bebal adalah lebih dahsyat daripada bodoh. Ia adalah satu kalimat yang menunjukkan tumpul otak, sukar mengerti, lambat menanggapi atau memahami sesuatu perkara, dan menurut Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka membawa juga pengertian melakukan aneka kesalahan berulang.

Akan tetapi apakah yang dimaksudkan oleh Syed Hussein yang terkenal benci rasuah dan perasuah itu dengan kata ‘bebal’. Beliau mula memperkenalkan istilah bebalisme dalam Dewan Masyarakat edisi Mac 1988.

Menurut Syed Hussein, bebalisme ini ‘bukan satu ideologi atau sistem kepercayaan atau kebudayaan atau falsafah’ tetapi ia adalah ‘orientasi pemikiran yang malas, tidak berfikir, tidak berlogik, kadang-kadang kasar, tidak ambil tahu, terlalu cepat percaya tanpa bukti, tidak saintifik, berhamburan, tiada haluan, pasif, tidak kreatif dan tiada tujuan yang terang.’

Semua anasir yang beliau sebutkan di atas akan kita jumpa di media sosial. Kita akan temukan di Facebook, X, Tiktok dan Threads. Apa sahaja yang disalurkan akan diulas sebagai satu komentar, atau ditelan bulat dan lonjong tanpa sebarang daya kritis. Tuduhan, fitnah, dakwaan palsu membiak dan beranak pinak dengan mudah di musim politik bergelora. Gejala bebalisme ini akan mudah dieksploitasi oleh pihak bertentangan dalam politik. Masing-masing akan menyebar informasi yang entah ya entah tidak.

Syed Hussein seterusnya mengatakan ‘bebalisme adalah lintah bagi pemikiran’. Ia tidak perlu diajarkan, atau dikemukakan secara teratur. Ia terjadi dengan sendiri dan ‘disebarkan sebagai satu trend’ dan ia dirujuk sebagai lintah oleh beliau lantaran pelaku atau si bebalis itu ‘bertindak melalui mental tanpa kesedaran’.

Oleh sebab ia adalah lintah bagi pemikiran, ia boleh melekap pada siapa pun. Kata Syed Hussein, ia ‘berada dalam berbagai-bagai golongan masyarakat; tidak kira umur, jantina, kebudayaan, bangsa, agama, falsafah, keadaan, waktu dan tempat’.

Apa yang menggerunkan ia adalah unsur utama yang menghalang pertumbuhan intelektual. Makanya, apabila penyokong Umno ramai-ramai ingin membantai Ummi, kita segera tahu dan mengesani bahawa rata-rata orang Umno ini terkait dengan fenomena bebalisme yang membimbangkan ini. Mungkin tidak semua, misalnya Zambry yang juga ahli Umno.
Syed Hussein juga mengaitkan bebalisme dengan ‘aliran fanatik’ iaitu mereka yang enggan menerima kebenaran dan fakta, dan terus-terusan memilih untuk percaya hal-hal bodoh dan tanpa dasar.
Apakah ciri-ciri bebalisme dan mereka yang menghidapinya, iaitu bebalis?

Menurut Syed Hussein, sang bebalis itu adalah; pertamanya mempertahankan kejahilan dan kedegilan. Keduanya mereka itu pemalas, enggan mengikuti hujah dan menganalisanya. Ketiganya, mereka selalunya bersikap acuh tak acuh, berbanding dengan daya usaha yang gigih dalam berfikir. Yang mana apa sahaja lambakan penipuan dan perdaya akan ‘diterima, berbagai-bagai pendapat, berbagai-bagai khurafat, berbagai- bagai keanehan dan keganjilan’.

Keempat, bebalisme ini menjelma kerana ada rasa diri itu ‘bersifat berkuasa benar (authoritarian) yang mana ini benar pada sesetengah ahli politik yang berasa mereka masih berkuasa atau lebih berkuasa dari rakyat. Itulah sebabnya dalam hal Ummi kita melihat beliau dibuli di dalam talian.
Kelima, mereka yang bebal itu ‘tidak suka merenung dan berfikir dan tidak suka menguji (non-experimental)’.

Keenamnya, tambah Syed Hussein, ‘satu ciri bebalisme adalah menghendaki orang lain mempercayai apa yang disarankan atau diperkatakan tanpa memberi sebab-sebab atau penjelasan yang cukup mengenai sesuatu yang luar daripada kebiasaan’.

Ketujuh, Syed Hussein sosiologis terkemuka negara pernah menulis, ‘bebalisme tidak suka kepada sifat teratur dan perbahasan secara rasional dan tidak menghargai kedua-duanya sama sekali. Apabila seorang bebalis bertindak secara rasional, ini adalah kerana pengaruh daripada kebiasaan dan bukan pemikiran mendalam secara rasional dan kerana terapan agama atau kuasa luar.’ Jika kita merenung ciri ini, kita akan mendapati terdapat sesetengah penyokong agamawan atau tokoh kanan tertentu gagal berfikir waras kerana hati serta penglihatan mereka telah dibutakan oleh ketaasuban.

Kelapan, golongan bebal ini akan cepat kita kesani iaitu ’apabila mereka bertanya, ia menampakkan kurangnya kefahaman mereka tentang prinsip-prinsip dan dengan itu soalan mereka menjadi sia-sia.’ Sebagai contoh dalam hal isu kepimpinan adat dan pertikaian kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, apa sahaja fakta yang dibawa bahawa Undang yang lama telah digantikan di Luak dan disahkan di Dewan Keadilan akan kekal dinafikan, dipermainkan dan ditolak. Mereka enggan berusaha mempelajari prinsip adat sedia ada, dan terus-terusan menghasut, memprovokasi dan mencabar institusi adat dan diraja di negeri itu.

Dan kesembilan, Syed Hussein mengatakan sang bebalis itu biasanya ‘antilogik, kusut pemikiran, subur dengan kurafat, tidak mengandungi rasa seni (unaesthetic), tidak mempunyai sikap memelihara, menerima segala sesuatu tanpa menimbang dengan akal, tidak mempedulikan hukum sebab (causation) dan hukum pertentangan (contradiction), bersikap kuasa-benar (authoritative), dan pemikiran malas, degil, serta buntu.’

Jika kita khuatir gejala bebalisme ini mewabak di Malaysia, kita perlu mengetahui mana asal puncanya. Apakah yang menyebabkan bebalisme ini? Menurut Syed Hussein ia bermula di rumah. Tulis beliau dalam rencana itu, ‘penghalang yang pertama ialah suasana di rumah'. Dalam erti kata lain, jika ibu bapa bodoh dan bengap, biasanya mereka gagal menumbuhkan suasana tidak bebal dalam rumah tangga. Alatas malahan mengatakan untuk mengetahui rumah itu penuh kebebalan atau tidak, memadai dinilai jika ‘keluarga terlalu menggalakkan sukan dan muzik’ dan ‘tidak membaca buku’. Ini kerana ‘pengetahuan intelektual tidak disanjung tinggi sebagaimana pengetahuan tentang agama dan adat’. Syed Hussein seterusnya menyatakan bukanlah setiap rumah perlu melahirkan intelektual; ‘walaupun kita tidak mengharap tiap-tiap orang atau tiap-tiap keluarga melahirkan watak intelektual, tetapi kita perlu berharap sebahagian keluarga dan anggota masyarakat dapat menghasilkan semangat intelektual tadi’.
Apa yang lebih menakutkan dalam masyarakat adalah bebalisme ini turut dibiakkan oleh ahli akademik yang mana itu perlu dibincangkan dalam tulisan lain.

Misalnya, Ketua Menteri Melaka, Ab Rauf Yusoh bakal menerima ijazah kedoktoran daripada Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) pada 21 Nov ini. Ketua menteri Melaka yang bakal bergelar doktor itu pernah menyeru penyokong dan rakyat yang menyayangi Najib supaya mengumpulkan dana bagi membantu melengkapkan RM 50 juta agar beliau dapat ditahan di rumah.

Mujur sangat-sangat bekas ketua hakim negara, Tengku Maimun Tuan Mat dilantik sebagai penyandang pertama Kursi Diraja Integriti dan Tadbir Urus Baik, UKM. Pelantikan beliau itu diperkenan dan dititahkan oleh Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz yang juga tersohor antirasuah dan korupsi.

Apa pun syukur nikmat Allah, ada Ummi Umairah Bakhit yang telah dididik dan diasuh di rumah yang betul, di sekolah yang betul, di universiti yang betul; dan membaca bahan-bahan yang betul sehingga mampu berfikir kritis dan tidak bodoh. Sebagai alumni Universiti Malaya saya berbangga dengan Ummi. Tambahan pengungkap kata Syed Hussein adalah sarjana di Universiti Malaya dan pernah menjadi felo penyelidik kanan di Institut Alam dan Tamadun Melayu (Atma) di UKM suatu masa dahulu.
Pun berapa ramai generasi baharu seperti Ummi Umairah Bakhit? Berapa ramai yang mengenali Syed Hussein Alatas. Buka media sosial anda dan lihat berapa dan betapa ramai bebalis di luar sana.

dc2ecfeed8750825: From Moaz Nair

The persistent, fractured politicking among Indian political leaders has devolved into a tragic spectacle of self-preservation, birthing a swarm of toothless, ego-driven factions that have completely abandoned the community’s most vulnerable.
For decades, these leaders have traded genuine community advancement for personal clout and minor cabinet crumbs, leaving working-class Indians politically homeless.

Ironically, as the Indian demographic footprint shrinks, the number of these redundant, self-serving political groups keeps multiplying — each shouting from its own small hill while achieving absolutely nothing of substance.

If these career politicians truly possess an ounce of genuine care for the marginalised, they must immediately halt their petty bickering, dismantle their hollow factions, and focus on delivering institutional, non-negotiable economic welfare.

Recent demographic data from the statistics department covering 2016 to 2026 lays bare a damning reality. In just one decade, the Indian component of the citizen population shrivelled from 7% to 6.5%. Representing roughly 5.8% of the total national population, ethnic Indians total about 2.1 million citizens.
Behind these dwindling percentages lies an unsettling truth: a minority community is fast becoming adrift from the mainstream of national development.

Approximately 38.7% of the community falls into the Bottom 40% (B40) income bracket, translating to 227,000 households. More alarming still, the data indicates that 10% of these B40 families — around 22,000 households — survive on less than RM2,000 a month in extreme precarity.
However, a shrinking population footprint must never be used as a political excuse for a diminished national commitment.

Instead, this demographic decline demands an immediate paradigm shift — shattering the status quo of lazy, generic handouts and replacing them with high-impact policy interventions built upon three non-negotiable pillars.
The 2027 budget attempts to tackle these imbalances, but its success will hinge on execution.
Equity, asset ownership, and economic empowerment

A shrinking population share inherently dilutes purchasing power and locks minority communities out of wealth accumulation. To bridge this widening wealth chasm, outdated asset ownership policies must be aggressively dismantled.
This means enforcing strict, mandatory quotas and dedicated housing funds to guarantee B40 Indian households affordable housing.
The 2027 budget confronts these capital deficits by channelling a combined RM150 million through Tekun Nasional and Amanah Ikhtiar Malaysia.

This includes a dedicated RM100 million Indian Community Entrepreneur Development Scheme to provide critical capital to small business owners, and RM50 million in microcredit loans customised to uplift Indian women entrepreneurs.
Ensuring families own homes and hold financial assets is vital to systematically engineering sustainable, multi-generational social mobility.
TVET overhaul and educational infrastructure

A radical technical and vocational education and training (TVET) overhaul and digital empowerment must disrupt a stagnant workforce. The brutal job market of tomorrow will show no mercy to obsolete skillsets.
Indian youth — particularly those trapped in forgotten suburban fringes and estates — must be aggressively channelled into high-tier TVET ecosystems.

The 2027 budget offers a vital fiscal upgrade here. The allocation for the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit (Mitra) has been boosted to RM150 million, specifically earmarked to help youths make the transition into high-skilled industrial pipelines. Furthermore, Indian youth must tap into the wider national RM8 billion TVET budget.

Equally foundational is confronting the historical deficits in education infrastructure. Malaysia’s 528 Tamil national-type primary schools (SJKT) carry a complex legacy, with 324 operating as government-assisted institutions sitting on private estate or community trust lands.

This has historically locked many schools out of direct development funding, leaving 68% of them without basic ICT laboratories. The 2027 budget addresses this digital divide with a RM50 million allocation for essential repairs, rewiring, and basic amenities, alongside full reconstruction priorities for severe emergencies like at SJKT Dengkil in Selangor and SJKT Gopeng in Perak.
Ruthless structural reform for targeted poverty alleviation
The survival of these policies hinges entirely on a ruthless structural reform of Mitra. For decades, fragmented agendas and redundant aid distribution have sabotaged state interventions.

Mitra must be stripped of bureaucracy and given absolute, transparent, and centralised power over data, funding, and execution. Armed with a unified database, cost-of-living aid, scholarships, and micro-business grants can finally bypass bureaucratic gridlock.

Crucially, the ultimate success of the budget for working-class Indians relies on broader macroeconomic shifts. The mandated minimum wage hike to RM2,000 per month starting June 2027 will immediately lift the community’s most vulnerable 22,000 households out of deep financial distress, especially when combined with the RM16 billion Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah cash aid pool.
Moving beyond salvation

Ultimately, the integrity of Malaysia’s future will be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable. Addressing this demographic collapse is not a bloodless numbers game on a spreadsheet; it is an urgent battle for socioeconomic justice.
By executing these progressive policy pillars, the country can transform a demographic challenge into a powerful reservoir of human capital.

However, relying solely on external political salvation is a failing strategy. If the Indian community is to survive as a relevant economic force in Malaysia’s shifting landscape, it must aggressively dismantle internal fatalism.

Upward mobility cannot be granted by policy alone. Real transformation demands that the community fiercely engineer its own self-upliftment — taking absolute ownership of its wealth, its trajectory, and its future generations.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

042dfe8c62606c77: Ilya Pavlov / UnsplashDetails have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline. The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed. The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time. What is PHP? PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes. The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites. PHP runs on the server rather than your personal computer. This means most of us interact with PHP every single day without ever seeing it. A timeline of concerns In August, a cybersecurity researchers from a company called Wiz used their own tools and the latest versions of Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT AI models to trawl through PHP’s massive codebase. The Wiz team were searching for hidden programming weaknesses that an attacker could chain together to take over a system running PHP simply by sending a carefully crafted request over the internet. Within a few days, they found ways to break into PHP-powered systems from Drupal and WordPress which are used in huge swathes of the web. Wiz contacted the PHP security team to let them know about the flaws they had found. By late September, the PHP developers confirmed that the issue existed, and quietly began working on a fix. In cybersecurity, the responsible thing to do when you find a bug is to keep it private until a patch is ready. This is because public disclosure could provide a detailed map for hackers to exploit. This appears to be what the PHP developers were planning. However, yesterday a user on popular industry website Hacker News let news slip about the security flaws before any patches were ready. Following the leak, PHP’s developers rushed to publicly confirm the issue on October 21, releasing emergency patches ahead of schedule. Implementing the patches is far from simple. Because PHP sits underneath thousands of third-party plugins, frameworks and managed hosting services, websites are only secure once every individual layer of the supply chain integrates and deploys the PHP fix. Why does this keep happening? Much of the internet is built on foundational technologies that were developed and maintained by hobbyist developers. Many rely on goodwill and donations rather than robust corporate funding. Many of these tools were first developed decades ago. They were never designed to safely support a world where millions of websites and billions of devices use them to handle sensitive and private data. Compounding this issue is the fact that maintenance is rarely a priority for organisations. All too often, companies have only the most basic knowledge about all the pieces of their supply chains – either physical or digital. Even in high profile cases such as this one, many businesses don’t even realise what software they depend on, let alone have any idea of how secure it actually is. What should you do? This issue is mainly one for people who maintain websites or manage technical infrastructure. For those people, the priority is clear: patch systems immediately when updates are available, and consider taking down critical systems from the internet until you can be confident about their security. For everyday internet users, these vulnerabilities affect the servers hosting websites rather than your personal device. However, because some sites may be temporarily compromised before they can patch, it is wise to be cautious about entering sensitive personal data on unfamiliar websites over the next few days. Major cloud providers and security firms are rolling out emergency filters, but the global scramble to secure the web is just beginning. Cybersecurity teams around the world are rushing to contain the damage. But the scope of this issue should be a wake-up call. Governments and businesses cannot ignore the resilience of their digital supply chains. Just as manufacturers track the suppliers of the physical components they depend upon, we should expect that digital infrastructure also traces every system and framework it depends on. Gathering this information is the first step for businesses and governments to truly understand how heavily their digital viability relies on underfunded, volunteer-maintained code. Until businesses treat funding open-source foundational tools as a critical security investment rather than a charity, these vulnerabilities will keep happening. Andrew Cullen is a board member at Music Technology Australia, a member of the World Intellectual Property Organizations AI Technical Exchange Committee, and the managing consultant at EthiCan.
d02e8a27185f940c: Protest helps close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we actually have

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Democracy is often presented as an orderly, structured system of representation and deliberation, colorless and linear like an organizational version of the faux-classical architecture so many democratic countries adopt for their government buildings. Voting leads to representatives, debates lead to votes on laws, participation leads to action, like columns leading to a pediment.

But democracy is not actually about cushy debating chambers or political speeches — or not only about that. Democracy means rule by the people, and in most of the systems we call democracies today, the people’s role is for the most part narrowed to voting, and often a curtailed, difficult, limited vote that does little for accountability or expressing preferences on specific issues.

Protest is one of the ways we close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we have. With protest, the people can express general emotional responses or very specific policy proposals; we can punctuate the long intervals of electoral cycles to influence government outside of the voting booth; and perhaps most importantly, we build coalitions and solidarity, forming a collective consciousness of our democratic responsibilities.

Voting is a single, standardized, and fairly isolated action. Protest, on the other hand, unfolds in dozens, if not hundreds, of permutations, letting us — the people — express our creativity along with our civic engagement. One of the wonderful things about this spotlight has been seeing the sheer range of capacity and ingenuity as people use protest to inspire others, express anger or determination, and pressure governments and other decision-makers.

Maybe the most obvious example of this in the spotlight is the collaborative article on protest music, with its examples of not just different songs, but different styles and approaches and even understanding of what it means to use music for advocacy. In Japan, young people are finding new paths into activism, like handing out placards, while the Cockroach Janta Party in India has used memes and online jokes to mobilize young people right from the start of the movement.

Severe oppression requires more creativity, as this article about the evolution of street art in Russia points out. Similarly, Russians — many of them in exile — used allusion and wordplay in online videos to get their messages across.

That raises the question, ably explored in this piece, about whether online and offline protest are equally effective, and what their different strengths and weaknesses are. And, if the digital world has enabled new forms of protest, it has also activated new means of repression. Our friends at Ranking Digital Rights contributed this well-researched article about the complicity of telecoms in internet shutdowns in Africa. This piece, from AlgorithmWatch, details the Russian surveillance software being used against protesters in Georgia. And the virtual world can be used to hijack, undermine, or redirect protest energy, as this case study from Funky Citizens in Romania details.

As vibrant as protests are in the moment, though, it’s also important to ask about the long-term impact, the consequences, both good and bad. The protests in Bangladesh two years ago were successful in the sense that they led to a change of government; this article asks whether that change of government led to a meaningful difference in democratic accountability. And this powerful piece from Nepal follows up with those involved in the Gen Z protests there last year, tracking the long-term impacts of injuries and trauma.

As with all our monthly spotlights, this one is in many ways about showing the common threads that link all of our countries, as well as the exceptions that can open us to new ideas or inspire us to a different kind of action. This spotlight is, then, a form of protest in its own right: a way of reasserting that protest is legitimate, important for democracy, and everywhere.
e3f519129b2e62b1: Whenever a minimum wage announcement falls short of public expectations, the political knee-jerk reaction is to aim all arrows at Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Yet, directing the blame solely at him misses the real dynamics behind Malaysia’s wage policy formulation.

First, consider how policy recommendations are shaped. Talent Corp and the human resources ministry paid RM1 million to a consulting firm specifically to research and recommend an appropriate minimum wage rate.
When the government relies on external subject-matter experts, paid handsomely with public funds, it acts on structured economic assessments rather than arbitrary political whims.
If the resulting figure feels inadequate to the working public, we must scrutinise the methodology, data and assumptions used by these highly paid consultants first.
The research, findings, and identity of these consultants ought to be made public for full transparency and proper scrutiny before rushing to condemn the prime minister.

Second, the relentless pushback from employer groups continues to stall wage growth. Business associations and industry groups routinely lobby against wage increases, warning of economic ruin and mass layoffs.

Their aggressive pushback invariably leads to exemptions and now deferred compliance for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), diluting the impact of wage reforms across major sectors of the economy.
Meanwhile, Anwar’s track record demonstrates a consistent commitment to raising worker compensation.
The minimum wage has risen 33% under the Madani government from RM1,500 in 2022 to RM2,000 in 2027. Graduates and semi-skilled workers will have a new minimum monthly salary of RM2,500.

Under Anwar’s administration, government-linked companies (GLCs) have actively led by example, setting a baseline living wage that was raised in Budget 2027 from RM3,100 to RM3,400. This upward revision reflects a genuine drive to ensure decent standards of living where the government holds direct leverage.

The true obstacles to a higher floor wage are not found in the prime minister’s office. The real villains in this story are the corporate lobbies constantly fighting wage increases and the consultants who produce conservative recommendations despite million-ringgit fees.

Rather than make Anwar the scapegoat, public discourse should demand accountability from the consultants who drafted the proposal and the employer groups who consistently undermine fair pay for Malaysian workers.

That said, according to research and analysis published in The Economist, governments should be cautious about aggressive minimum wage hikes due to mounting evidence of hidden economic distortions and better alternative policy tools.

Research from Nobel Prize winner David Card and others in the 1990s showed that the negative impact of minimum wages was overstated and job-losses were offset by higher spending and economic activity.

Recent studies, such as evaluations of sharp minimum wage increases in places like Seattle, show that high-wage floors can slow down the hiring of low-wage workers and reduce total work hours rather than cause immediate mass layoffs.
To offset higher baseline pay, employers often resort to unpredictable scheduling, fewer workplace perks, or higher output demands that can lead to increased workplace accidents.
High minimum wages are a blunt tool for fighting poverty because many minimum-wage earners live in households with high-earning family members.
Businesses, especially in labour-intensive or low-margin sectors, frequently pass higher wage costs onto consumers through rising prices, triggering affordability pressures.

The Economist highlights alternatives such as in-work tax credits, the progressive wage policy (PWP) in Malaysia or reverse income taxes, as superior approaches because they target low-income households directly without creating the same economic distortions or hidden costs.
Regular readers of this column will be familiar with these ideas because I have advocated them for many years and they have recently been adopted by Bersama.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock “may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target,” and told them to be on the lookout for “emotional confrontations” between people who oppose surveillance and government officials, according to a copy of the warning obtained by 404 Media.

The warning, obtained by 404 Media, was issued by the Orange County Intelligence Assessment Center (OCIAC)—a government fusion center—in July to police in California. 404 Media recently obtained the bulletin using a Freedom of Information Act request.

This surveillance bulletin to cops is the latest evidence that police around the country have been told to be on edge during public meetings where people are participating in democracy and utilizing their First Amendment rights about unpopular things the government is doing. We have reported on a spate of people being illegally arrested for extremely minor procedural violations or for cursing at city council meetings about Flock and data centers while participating in constitutionally protected activities.

The warning is similar to others obtained by 404 Media and other journalists about the broader DeFlock movement and vandalism of Flock surveillance cameras. But this warning specifically tells police that there have been “no specific and credible threats found” related to city council meetings about Flock, but warns they should be on the lookout anyway. The warning noted that anti surveillance organizers could have been emboldened by the news that the Los Angeles Police Department ended its Flock contract, and may expect other local governments to do the same. The LAPD’s decision was “providing organizers and participants with a high-profile local example that could increase turnout and place additional public pressure on City Council members” to end their Flock contracts, the bulletin claims.

“City-hosted events (i.e., city council meetings) may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target. Partners are encouraged to review for signs of suspicious activity,” the warning reads. This suspicious activity includes “excessive clothing,” “unusual questions or behavior,” people loitering,” or “unattended bags or packages.”

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The warning goes on to say that genuine interest in ending mass surveillance at a city council meeting “may present public safety risks,” which includes “large turnout exceeding room capacity,” “emotional confrontations,” counterdemonstrations,” “media presence,” “social media amplification,” and “disruption of council proceedings.”
Here is a full excerpt of the portion of the warning about protected activities that could apparently “present public safety risks:”

Large turnout exceeding room capacity: If organizers mobilize significantly more attendees than the council chambers can accommodate, this can lead to long lines, frustrated attendees, overflow areas, or delays in the meeting.

Emotional confrontations: Because the issue involves surveillance, privacy, immigration concerns, and public safety, speakers and attendees may have strong emotions. Verbal confrontations between supporters and opponents are more likely than at routine council meetings.
Counterdemonstrations: Individuals who support the Flock camera program or emphasize its crime-fighting benefits may attend and express opposing views, increasing the potential for verbal conflict.
Traffic and parking impacts: A well-attended meeting can create localized congestion around City Hall before and after the meeting.
Media presence: Local television, newspapers, livestreamers, and independent journalists may attend because the issue has recently received regional media coverage.
Social media amplification. Attendees may livestream or record interactions. Minor disputes can quickly spread online, increasing public attention.
Disruption of council proceedings. Possible issues include:Interrupting speakers
Shouting from the audience
Refusing to yield the podium after time limits
Coordinated chanting inside the chambers
Attempts to delay or prevent the meeting from continuing

Physical altercations: Heated disagreements between attendees with opposing viewpoints could escalate into minor physical altercations, particularly during emotionally charged interactions before, during, or after the meeting.

Targeted threats or intimidation: Any credible threats, harassment, or intimidation directed toward elected officials, city staff, organizers, or attendees should be treated as a significant public safety concern and evaluated promptly.

Extremist-related activity: Although there is no publicly available information indicating extremist involvement, politically contentious events may attract isolated individuals seeking to promote unrelated ideological causes.
We have seen numerous people illegally arrested around the country for speaking slightly too long, talking out of turn, or for cursing at city council members, none of which are illegal activities.

“The OCIAC recognizes that Americans have constitutionally protected rights to assemble, speak, and petition the government,” the warning ends. “The OCIAC safeguards these rights and only reports on First Amendment protected activities for operational planning in the interest of assuring the safety and security of the demonstrators and the public.”

c1afa369535ff9e0: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

9b117c793d41b661: President Donald Trump's offer to pay out $5,000 checks if Republicans win belongs to a long political tradition of cash for votes. AP Photo/Mark SchiefelbeinPolitics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win. President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “DOGE dividend” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues, and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans. But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view. For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races. I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote. Why vote buying rarely works The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia. By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants. Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s. But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes. If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence. Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent. As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “Against the Machine.” The importance of competition There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops. First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights. This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos.” In Mexico’s 2018 election, the PAN party, whose flags are pictured here, ran into opposition in Nuevo Laredo due to its vote-buying attempts. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets: Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision. Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret. It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment. Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it. Bringing it home Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely. Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate. There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism. The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.” At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vote to Republican. In theory, there is one way Trump’s offer could succeed. Research shows that buying turnout, rather than trying to change vote choices, is routinely effective. But all the examples come from countries where party officials actively monitor who comes to the polls. Without that surveillance, which is illegal in the U.S., the free-rider problem could bedevil turnout as well. But whether enacted or not, the promise of cash for votes has a big downside for democracy. It means that no one will know whether victorious Republican candidates won this November because Americans preferred their policies and gave them a mandate – or because they expected to get paid. Kenneth Greene's research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, the University of Texas at Austin, and the Mellon Foundation.
05c8eb78562a8d38: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Introducing: the Impossible issue

We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.

That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.

Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration.

How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster

In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.

The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.
—James Temple
MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world

“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.

MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.

5b3ce3d240be4172: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”

I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)

My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.

If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.
We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious.

Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.

We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.

It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.

Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.
So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.
I hope you enjoy the ride.

807cd6cdd4d4152d: From P Sundramoorthy

The high-profile investigation into the MBI International Group investment scheme raises a fundamental question about Malaysia’s response to major financial crime: what happens after arrests, raids, and the seizure or freezing of billions of ringgit in assets?
Under Op Northern Star, police announced the arrests of individuals suspected of facilitating the movement or laundering of funds linked to the alleged investment fraud.
By May 2025, authorities reported that 17 people were detained and assets worth approximately RM3.81 billion had been seized or frozen.
Subsequent reporting in January 2026 indicated that 23 people were arrested, with authorities pursuing the forfeiture of hundreds of properties and funds held in bank accounts.

These are significant developments. However, the public deserves clarity about whether investigations are progressing towards lawful outcomes and whether affected investors can realistically expect to recover their losses.
The MBI case should not be judged solely by the number of arrests or the value of assets seized. The real test is what follows.

Complex financial crime investigations require investigators to trace funds, establish individual responsibilities, examine corporate transactions and determine whether assets represent proceeds of unlawful activities.
The reported international dimension of the MBI case adds further challenges, including obtaining foreign evidence and coordinating with overseas enforcement agencies.

An arrest does not establish guilt, and a frozen asset does not automatically represent criminal proceeds. Similarly, release from remand does not necessarily mean a suspect has been cleared or that an investigation has ended.
However, these distinctions should not become a reason for prolonged public uncertainty.
Transparency without compromising investigations

When those previously detained in high-profile investigations return to their daily activities or retain prominent business and social positions, questions inevitably arise. Some may assume allegations have been dismissed, while others may suspect preferential treatment for influential individuals.

Neither conclusion should be drawn merely from a person's release or continued public presence. The presumption of innocence must be respected, and allegations must be established through proper legal proceedings.
The police should provide periodic updates while the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission should clarify the status of any related investigation within its jurisdiction.
Where legally permissible, updates should explain whether investigation papers have been referred to prosecutors and whether charges or asset forfeiture proceedings have commenced.

Where investigations have concluded or decisions have been made not to pursue particular individuals, appropriate clarification should be provided, subject to legal restrictions and the rights of those concerned.
Victims must not be forgotten

Perhaps the most important consideration is the position of investors who lost money through the MBI scheme. Announcements of billions of ringgit in seized or frozen assets may create expectations that investors will eventually recover their losses.
However, the value of seized assets does not necessarily represent the amount available for distribution to victims.
Assets may be subject to competing claims, ownership disputes and forfeiture proceedings. Their eventual recovery and distribution depend on applicable law and the outcomes of legal proceedings.
Authorities should communicate realistic expectations about asset recovery and explain, within legal limits, what mechanisms are available to address victims' claims.
Op Metal a broader lesson

The importance of following investigations through to their outcomes is also illustrated by Op Metal, a separate MACC operation launched in July 2025 targeting an alleged scrap metal and electronic waste smuggling syndicate.

Authorities seized assets worth over RM183 million and froze company and individual bank accounts containing approximately RM51 million. The suspected activities were estimated to have caused the government more than RM950 million in lost export tax revenue over six years.
Op Metal is unrelated to the MBI investment scheme investigation. However, it reinforces a broader lesson: seizures and enforcement announcements are only part of the process.

The MBI case warrants particular attention because of the financial losses suffered by investors and the importance of maintaining confidence in Malaysia's handling of major investment-related fraud allegations.
It presents an opportunity for Malaysian authorities to demonstrate that complex, cross-border financial crime can be confronted with determination, professionalism and transparency.
Ultimately, the public does not expect investigators to reveal everything, but it does expect them to explain what can responsibly be disclosed, demonstrate progress and communicate lawful outcomes.
Justice must extend beyond the headlines.
P Sundramoorthy is a criminologist at the Centre for Policy Research at Universiti Sains Malaysia and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

7eac5dc4d24bb6eb: Malaysia's automotive industry has become an interesting battleground between Japan and China, two of the world's great carmaking powers. And the contest is being played out through our national carmakers, Proton and Perodua.
Proton has the backing of Zhejiang Geely, one of China's most technologically advanced automotive groups while Perodua has the support of Daihatsu and, behind it, the industrial might of Toyota.
Both partnerships have been successful, but the arrival of electric vehicles (EV) has changed the rules of the game.

China has taken a commanding lead in EV technology, battery production and manufacturing costs. Japan, despite its dominance of the global automotive industry for decades, has been more cautious about committing itself to battery electric vehicles beyond hybrids.
That puts Perodua in a particularly interesting position.

An important insight into Japan's intentions came in May when its ambassador to Malaysia, Noriyuki Shikata, described Perodua as one of the best examples of a successful Japanese-Malaysian joint venture. More significantly, he disclosed that Japan's economy, trade and industry ministry had decided to extend financial support for a new Perodua-led project.
Shikata also observed that Perodua was entering a new stage of innovation, developing solutions in Malaysia that Japan itself was interested in learning about.

Now, that is an interesting statement coming from the representative of one of the world's most sophisticated automotive nations. For more than three decades in the auto industry, we have regarded the Japanese as the teachers and Malaysians as the students.
Could the relationship now be evolving into something more equal?
From petrol to electric
Consider what Perodua has achieved.

Starting with the modest Kancil in 1994, it has grown into Malaysia's largest carmaker, commanding roughly 40% of our domestic market. Its success was built on affordable, reliable petrol-engine cars, efficient manufacturing and a formidable local supplier network.
The question is whether Perodua can translate these strengths into the electric age.

Its first home-grown EV, the QV-E, represents a bold but expensive undertaking. Unlike Proton, which can draw upon Geely's existing EV platforms and economies of scale, Perodua has invested heavily in developing its own product.
The difference is fundamental. Proton benefits from China's enormous EV ecosystem. Perodua is attempting to develop Malaysian engineering capabilities while building a new supply chain.
Market reception

The QV-E encountered a difficult market reception, with pricing and battery leasing arrangements initially raising questions among buyers. Subsequent price reductions have made it more competitive, but they also illustrate the formidable economics of EV manufacturing.
This is where government policy becomes important. Should Malaysia provide targeted financial assistance to Perodua to develop its EV capabilities?

I believe there is a strong case for doing so, provided the assistance is directed towards research, engineering, local components and technology development rather than simply subsidising car prices as China did for 5 years

There is an even stronger argument if Japan is prepared to participate. Toyota and Daihatsu possess enormous experience in manufacturing efficiency, quality control and supplier development. Combining these strengths with Perodua's local engineering ambitions could create something genuinely valuable.
It would also give Japan an opportunity to develop affordable EV technologies for Asean markets, where price sensitivity remains a major consideration.
Supply chains

We should not overlook that China already enjoys significant advantages in battery technology and scale. Perodua's QV-E itself uses batteries from China's CATL, among the world's biggest maker of EV batteries.
The modern automotive industry depends on international supply chains.
The objective should not be to manufacture every component in Malaysia. It should be to develop technologies and industrial capabilities in which Malaysians can become genuinely competitive.

Nor should this become another exercise in protecting a national carmaker from competition. The government must insist on measurable results, greater localisation, export potential and meaningful Malaysian intellectual property.
Green technology

The transition towards EVs should not be measured solely by the number of electric vehicles sold. The environmental impact of automotive manufacturing, energy consumption, battery production, material sourcing and recycling must also be considered.
Government R&D assistance should therefore include the development and adoption of green technologies and cleaner manufacturing processes throughout Malaysia's automotive industry.
This could include energy-efficient production systems, AI-based energy optimisation, battery recycling, resource efficiency and technologies that reduce industrial emissions.
Such initiatives would not only support environmental sustainability but also improve the competitiveness of Malaysian automotive suppliers in international markets.
Measurable benefits

A proper mechanism should be established to assess the actual national benefits generated by government R&D assistance. Malaysia's New Incentive Framework, introduced in 2026, already moves towards linking investment incentives with measurable economic outcomes.

Rather than creating overlapping subsidy schemes, the government should examine how existing mechanisms can be strengthened and better coordinated to support automotive AI, strategic R&D and green industrial development.
The Japanese ambassador's remarks suggest that Japan sees something worth supporting in Perodua. Malaysia should recognise the opportunity.
Rather than viewing Proton and Perodua simply as two national carmakers competing for domestic sales, perhaps we should see them as two different pathways into the future of automotive manufacturing.
One draws upon China's extraordinary scale and speed. The other could build upon Japan's engineering discipline and Malaysia's own industrial experience.
If both succeed, Malaysia will be the winner. And the one which exports the most is the champion.

Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, "Google built-in" is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it's the other way around.

9a892035dd55c082: From Shahrim Tamrin
I welcome Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research (Miros) chairman Wong Shaw Voon’s renewed call to raise the minimum age for a motorcycle licence from 16 to 18.
But this is hardly a new proposal. It has been under discussion since 2018.
Malaysia needs neither another round of deliberations nor another announcement without a clear outcome. It needs transparency, a policy decision and the political will to act.

In May 2018, during Loke Siew Fook’s first term as transport minister, the transport ministry sought public feedback on the minimum licensing age, with Miros and relevant road safety authorities involved. The exercise ran until September, but its findings have never been made publicly available through official channels.

I obtained a summary of Miros’s findings after requesting it two years ago. The results were mixed. The online exercise involved 4,005 members of the public and 11 experts, while a separate survey covered 4,158 respondents.

Although Miros reported majority support among online participants for raising the age to 18, many motorcycle riders and secondary school students opposed the change. Some students even suggested lowering the age.
The findings do not establish a blanket public mandate for change. They establish something more fundamental: evidence was collected and the public deserves to know what became of it.

The presentation also reported that 80% of boys and 86% of girls surveyed rode to school without a motorcycle licence. Of 181 boys aged 16, only three held one. Meanwhile, 58% of students said their parents did not stop them from riding.

These figures concern the students surveyed, not all Malaysian schoolchildren. Nevertheless, they expose a problem that raising the licensing age alone cannot solve. Even a 13-year-old can ride an illegally obtained “kapcai”.
Wong himself has cautioned that raising the age will achieve little without effective enforcement against underage riders.
Licensing reform must, therefore, go hand in hand with enforcement, parental accountability and controls over access to motorcycles.
The paper trail

On Oct 8, 2019, police proposed a new B3 motorcycle licensing category at the National Road Safety Council’s 60th annual general meeting. The proposal envisaged restricting young riders to motorcycles of 70cc or below, or low-powered electric alternatives, to curb illegal street racing and improve road safety.

Recorded as Item 9.4 in the meeting minutes, the proposal was referred to the transport ministry. Years later, the public is still waiting to learn whether it was seriously considered and why it produced no clear policy outcome.

On Nov 25, 2021, Miros’s board backed a related but distinct proposal to study restricting young riders to motorcycles below 90cc. Recorded as Board Paper LPM 2-52 under Item 52.4(2), it was approved by the board, including its then chairman Suret Singh.
One proposal concerned a licensing category; the other concerned research into engine-capacity restrictions.
Nearly five years later, the study’s status remains unclear. Was it completed? What did it find? Were recommendations submitted to the transport ministry? If the study was not completed, why not?

In August 2024, the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (Suhakam) children’s commissioner Farah Nini Dusuki sought an update on the B3 proposal and urged the transport ministry and road transport department (JPJ) to expedite legislation addressing motorcycle purchases by unlicensed riders. She also highlighted the unresolved status of the Miros study.
A study endorsed by the board should not become an administrative mystery.
Human cost
Suhakam has highlighted the risks faced by underage motorcyclists, including 87 children aged six to 10 who died while riding motorcycles rather than as pillion passengers.
Children do not acquire motorcycles by themselves. Adults may purchase them, provide access or knowingly permit illegal riding. Sellers and the wider regulatory framework also warrant scrutiny.

Section 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001 addresses neglect likely to cause physical injury to a child, while Section 39(5) of the Road Transport Act 1987 addresses causing or permitting a child below 16 to drive. Their application depends on the circumstances and relevant legal requirements.
Parental accountability matters, but it must not become a substitute for institutional accountability.

The government should disclose the status of legislation reportedly being developed to regulate motorcycle purchases by unlicensed individuals, explain outstanding obstacles and provide a timetable. The problem extends beyond teenagers riding kapcai – unlicensed adults can also access more powerful motorcycles.
I call on the transport ministry, JPJ and Miros to:
Publish the 2018 survey. Release its methodology, detailed findings and recommendations, while protecting respondents’ personal information where necessary.
Account for Board Paper LPM 2-52. Confirm whether the study was completed, publish its findings and explain what action followed.
Disclose the proposed legislation’s status. Set a timetable for regulating motorcycle purchases by unlicensed buyers and establish enforceable safeguards.

Set a timetable for licensing reform. Decide whether to raise the minimum age to 18 and seriously consider the B3 proposal, alongside proportionate power restrictions for young and inexperienced riders, effective enforcement and meaningful parental accountability.
Wong deserves credit for returning the issue to the agenda. In my years covering Miros, I have seen board recommendations stall before reaching the ministerial table.
It remains unclear whether Board Paper LPM 2-52, or any recommendation arising from it, ever reached the transport minister in a form requiring a decision. That, too, warrants an explanation.

Research cannot improve road safety if recommendations fail to travel from the boardroom to the ministerial table. Nor can policy succeed if it exists only in announcements, meeting minutes and presentation slides.
Malaysia is not short of studies, recommendations or press statements. It is short of visible follow-through.
Publish the evidence. Account for the decisions made and those left unmade. Set a timetable and act. The public has waited long enough, and too many children have already paid the price.
Shahrim Tamrin is a sustainable transport and road safety activist and former Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research board member.
