a7aafe25914aada1: Billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai and Elon Musk, pictured here at President Donald Trump's 2025 inauguration, have seen their wealth soar thanks to the stock market boom and beneficial tax changes. Chip Somodevilla/Pool Photo via APThe buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability, but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment. A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this. This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs. I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality. Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%. Inequality by the numbers Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow. The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999. These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data. But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026. Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories. Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall. The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom. How taxes play a role Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive, often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats. The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth. Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940. While many voters cite affordability as a top concern, concerns over inequality have increasingly been part of this debate. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from. Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership, allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash, usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares. By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%. The new drivers of inequality Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed. One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs. The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil. Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%. This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “A Brief History of Equality,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.” Markus Schneider does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
0bf81f6de8a00451: Would this bother you? 500px/Getty ImagesImagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like “the one” when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it. Consumers do this all the time. They replace phones that still work, furniture with a scratch and sweaters with a small snag. Often, what has changed is how people see these items. We are marketing researchers who study why people buy, use and get rid of stuff. This obsession with perfection began when one of us, Aprajita Gautam, moved from India to the U.S. in 2019. She was struck by how different the culture of buying and owning things was in the two countries. In our peer-reviewed research paper, published in August 2026 in the Journal of Consumer Research, we identified one reason for this pattern: Some people care much more than others about having flawless things. We call this penchant a desire for perfect products. Not the same as perfectionism We began by interviewing 17 people in Austin, Texas, in 2023. They included real estate agents, entrepreneurs, stay-at-home mothers and people employed by an nonprofit that promotes reuse. We asked them about their possessions and what made things seem perfect or imperfect. We then surveyed about 540 more people, some online and some in a university research lab. The results suggested that people who strongly preferred flawless items had more elaborate ideas about what their ideal product was and were sensitive to even small deviations from those ideas. Their standards also kept rising. Seeing something better than what they owned could raise the bar further for them. Next, we developed questions to assess how much people care about having flawless possessions. We used people’s answers to determine how strongly they desired perfect products. We also found that this tendency is related to but distinct from perfectionism. While perfectionists hold themselves to high or even impossible standards, people who want perfect stuff hold what they buy and own to lofty standards. You might easily shrug off a bad day at the office but be far less forgiving of a scratch on your new coffee table. For people who feel they have to own perfect products, even a small imperfection can overshadow everything else they like about something they own. Finally, we conducted 12 experiments where we recruited participants – University of Texas at Austin students and online workers participating in crowdsourcing marketplaces – to test the behavioral effects of the desire for perfect possessions. It can affect how you shop In our first online experiment, we asked 402 consumers across the country to imagine booking a hotel in California’s Napa Valley using filters like those on travel websites, such as star rating, Wi-Fi or a spa. Consumers who desired perfect products used more filters and set higher cutoffs, narrowing their search to hotels that came closer to meeting their standards. Newness itself also had value for them. In another online experiment with 301 consumers, those who cared most about owning flawless possessions were quicker to upgrade to the latest iPhone, even when it offered little real improvement over the previous one. This urge can be costly. It can mean paying extra for something new when the old one works fine, or spending more time searching for a product that meets every standard that may not actually matter. If you can live with imperfections, you can buy some of your stuff used. Moment/Getty Images Makes people less open to repairs This preference also affects what people do with the stuff they already own. In our next online experiment, we asked 1,004 U.S. participants to chose between two options: an insulated coffee mug and an insulated water bottle. When told that the product they chose had a small dent on the bottom, those who were most bothered by flaws in their possessions were more likely to swap it for the other option. We found a similar pattern with repairs. In an online experiment with 601 consumers, we found that those who want to own perfect products were less interested in fixing a broken keyboard when the replacement key wouldn’t match the color of the other keys. This highlights a problem with repairs that isn’t usually part of discussions about sustainable consumption: Fixing something can restore its function without necessarily making it look as good as new. A factor for donations Consumers with exacting standards for their things also applied their high standards to items they were getting rid of. In an experiment we conducted in a university behavioral lab, we asked 339 students to help with a “Clean Out Your Closet” drive. They examined pieces of clothing that others had discarded and sorted them into two bins: one to donate and one to recycle. Those who strongly preferred flawless items were less likely to donate imperfect but still usable clothing. This attitude can shorten a product’s useful life. That finding has implications for sustainability. Much of the academic research about sustainable consumption focuses on what people buy. But another way to consume less is to keep products in use longer. That becomes harder if small imperfections make otherwise useful products seem less valuable. Learning to value imperfection Our research suggests that how someone responds to flaws in their possessions can vary depending on what those flaws mean to them. We were inspired in part by the Japanese concept of wabi-sabi, which finds beauty and value in imperfection and change. In our final online experiment, 1,203 consumers learned about hoodies with subtle variations in color and pattern. When those variations were described as making each hoodie unique, consumers who love having perfect products responded less negatively to them. A mark on a well-used object can be seen as a flaw, but it can also become part of its history. And replacing products because of minor imperfections can lead consumers to waste their money. None of this means consumers should keep everything forever. Mugs break and clothing and shoes get worn out. Sometimes people simply want something new. But consider that bag again. Its scuffs could mean it is no longer the perfect bag you originally bought. Or they could mean you’ve carried it hundreds of times because you like it. 7a9898c01ede12be: If Bersama were to contest 15 seats in the Melaka polls on Nov 14, it is certain to take away votes from PKR, DAP and Amanah.

It is not too late to rescind a move that bodes ill for a future in which Bersama ought to have a vital role in making the reforms long sought by Pakatan Harapan (PH) a reality, thereby setting on course the creation of a different country from the prevailing one, whose contours are likely to be reinforced by the right-wingers of Umno and the Islamists of PAS.

As if the good fairies have decided to play a hand in steering things towards an outcome both congenial for Bersama and beneficial to PH, Bersama’s co-founder Nik Nazmi Nik Ahmad is in a spot of bother that may well throw him off stride for GE16.

The khalwat case he is facing may well disqualify the former MP for Setiawangsa from being the constituency’s first Bersama MP at GE16. Prior to the case’s inception, Nik Nazmi was on course, after resigning as PKR MP for Setiawangsa, to being returned at GE16, under Bersama’s colours, as the seat’s MP.
Now that probability is dimmed by what hangs over him at the shariah court.

This is grist for the argument that Bersama ought to draw in its tentacles and play to its strengths. There is no point in splitting votes at the Melaka polls and persisting in attacking PKR and Anwar Ibrahim on the stumps, as Bersama has been known to do from the time the party set sail.

When Rafizi Ramli and Nik Nazmi launched a new political vehicle by forming Bersama, it was clear the pair were on course, heading up to GE16, which must be called by February 2028, to carve off something like 10 of the 31 parliamentary seats that PKR won at GE15 in November 2022.
Their incumbents were pro-Rafizi and will likely be won again by the same coterie if re-contested by them.
Bersama will want to contest a number of other seats held by PKR MPs, but not significantly more.

Bersama went into the Johor state polls in July with hopes of making some gains. They wound up with nothing but lost deposits and were suitably chagrined to not want to contest in the subsequent Negeri Sembilan polls.
But now Bersama fancies its chances in Melaka: it has not learnt its lesson that what plays in the Klang Valley does not exactly play outside its highly urban and urbane precincts.
The Nik Nazmi khalwat case is a symptom of Bersama’s presumptuousness.
The party must play within its strengths.
And wait for the realisation to congeal that after Anwar, it is Rafizi who should resuscitate the fallen reformasi colours.
Hence, there isn’t much point in alienating its putative allies in PKR, DAP and Amanah by going solo and splitting votes at the Melaka polls and elsewhere.
What has happened to Nik Nazmi should introduce some grains of sand into Bersama’s balm of complacent assumption.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

6c941b9db65caba4: Hidup berjiran memang ada macam-macam ragam.

Ada jiran yang baik hati, suka menolong, ringan tulang dan mengambil berat tentang orang sekeliling. Ada juga jiran yang kita tidak begitu kenal, tetapi tidak pernah mendatangkan masalah. Masing-masing menjaga hal sendiri.
Ada yang sudah bertahun-tahun tinggal berdepan-depan, tetapi sekadar angkat tangan dan senyum. Tidak pernah berbual. Janji tidak menyusahkan orang lain, kita baik-baik sahaja.
Ada juga yang langsung tidak mahu memandang, apatah lagi bertegur sapa. Tetapi selagi tidak membuat susah kepada orang lain, itu pun tidak mengapa.
Yang susah apabila mendapat jiran yang selalu buat hal. Entah apa penyakitnya, suka membuat orang lain tidak senang.
Laman rumahnya bersemak-samun sehingga mungkin menjadi tempat pembiakan nyamuk. Ditambah pula suka membuat bising tidak mengenal waktu. Sudah tentu kita semua akan rimas dan serba salah.
Apabila ditegur, dia tidak berubah. Silap-silap kita pula diajak bertumbuk.

Bukan dia sahaja yang menyusahkan, seluruh keluarganya pun sama. Anak-anak bukan main nakal, suka mengganggu rakan sebaya. Emaknya pula bermulut jahat, suka mengata sana-sini. Tidak boleh tengok orang lain lebih sedikit, dinaikkan pula hantaran menyindir di media sosial.

Lama-kelamaan, seluruh kejiranan bengang dan terganggu dengan perangai jiran seperti ini sehingga masalah itu terpaksa dibawa ke mesyuarat persatuan penduduk, malah memerlukan campur tangan ketua masyarakat atau pihak berkuasa.
Tetapi masalah tetap tidak selesai. Dia masih tidak berubah.
Apabila ada pihak datang sebagai wakil pendamai untuk memujuk, pandai pula dia mengajar orang lain. Disuruhnya kita bersabar. Katanya, hidup berjiran perlu ada toleransi.

Kemudian dia merengek dan berlakon menjadi mangsa. Orang lain semuanya salah, dia sahaja yang betul. Disebut-sebut dan diungkit-ungkit pula apa yang sudah dilakukannya selama ini. Kononnya dia juga ada jasa di kawasan kejiranan.
Ini bukan cerita rekaan.
Kalau kita tinggal di kampung, rumah pangsa rakyat atau taman perumahan, memang ada orang jenis begini. Kadang-kadang kita pun tidak faham bagaimana orang seperti mereka boleh wujud di muka bumi ini.
Ketika orang lain sepakat dan boleh hidup aman, dia muncul mengocak ketenangan. Apa kepuasan yang dia dapat, kita pun tidak boleh hendak hadam.
Takkanlah tidak tahu bahawa dalam beragama memang ada bab adab hidup berjiran. Kita dituntut supaya menghormati jiran, menjaga hubungan baik dan tidak menyusahkan orang lain.

Tetapi hubungan baik sepatutnya berjalan dua hala. Tidak bolehlah seorang jiran sentiasa diminta bersabar sedangkan jiran yang menyebabkan masalah sewenang-wenangnya melakukan apa sahaja yang dia suka.
Hal-hal mudah pun sepatutnya kita boleh fikir sendiri.
Jangan halang pintu keluar masuk rumah jiran dengan kereta kita. Jangan biarkan haiwan peliharaan membuang najis merata-rata di atas jalan atau di rumah jiran.
Pada musim perayaan, kalau boleh elakkan membakar mercun apabila sudah masuk waktu tidur. Ada anak kecil dan orang tua yang tidak sihat, pasti mereka akan terkejut.
Jangan pula bakar sampah sehingga asap masuk ke rumah jiran.
Ini semua perkara yang kita boleh fikir sendiri.
Tetapi nanti sekejap.
Bagaimana kalau mereka sebenarnya tahu perbuatan itu menyusahkan orang lain, tetapi tidak mempedulikannya?
Lebih teruk lagi jika mereka mendapat keuntungan daripada perbuatan itu, sedangkan orang lain terpaksa menanggung akibatnya.
Ini bukan lagi soal kesedaran atau common sense. Ini sudah masuk soal tanggungjawab.
Rasulullah SAW bersabda, maksudnya:
“Demi Allah, tidak beriman! Demi Allah, tidak beriman! Demi Allah, tidak beriman!”
Apabila ditanya siapakah orang itu, Baginda menjawab:
“Orang yang jirannya tidak berasa aman daripada gangguannya.”
(Riwayat al-Bukhari, no. 6016)

Apabila dikatakan jiran, ia jelas tidak terbatas kepada kaum dan agama. Jiran ialah mereka yang paling dekat di sekeliling kita, yang bersama-sama menjadi sebahagian daripada sesebuah kelompok atau komuniti.
Begitulah Islam mementingkan kesejahteraan jiran tetangga. Kita dituntut berbuat baik kepada jiran walaupun berbeza warna kulit dan kepercayaan.
Tetapi watak pengacau tetap ada.
Bukan di rumah sahaja. Di dalam bilik darjah, pasti ada seorang watak pengacau atau kaki buli. Di pejabat pula ada kaki mengadu domba.
Malah, di peringkat dunia pun ada negara yang kita panggil jiran tetapi suka buat hal.
Tiap-tiap tahun rumah kita dimasuki asap gara-gara jiran membuat pembakaran “di halamannya”. Kita dan jiran-jiran lain sudah puas mengeluh, tetapi dia tidak peduli.
Apa kita hendak buat dengan mereka?
Sikap tidak mempedulikan pihak lain ini cukup membuatkan kita tertekan. Kita bingung dan mati kutu. Sampai bilakah keadaan ini akan berterusan? Bilakah pula mereka akan sedar dan berubah?
Maka, setelah puas mengeluh, ayuhlah kita berdoa kepada tuhan agar pintu akal mereka terbuka dan mereka menjadi lebih bijak sedikit.
Berdoalah sungguh-sungguh sebelum terlambat. Sebelum keamanan dan kesihatan kita musnah.
Bukan apa.
Saya sudah bosan dengan jerebu ini.
Tolonglah, wahai jiran!
Bebaskan kami daripada kekaburan yang melemaskan paru-paru ini.
Kami semakin tidak tahan!

773c6020d7b35831: From Moaz Nair
Not too long ago, Negeri Sembilan stood proud as a bastion of political tranquillity amidst a turbulent national landscape.

Under the previous Barisan Nasional–Pakatan Harapan coalition government led by former menteri besar Aminuddin Harun, the state enjoyed a rare commodity in modern Malaysian politics: absolute administrative stability.

Today, that hard-won stability has been recklessly squandered. Negeri Sembilan now finds itself ensnared in a historic, multi-layered constitutional crisis born entirely of the current government’s own missteps.

For the voters, legal experts, and everyday citizens witnessing this paralysis, the contrast between past order and present dysfunction could not be starker. The memory of the previous BN-PH framework is fast becoming the definitive benchmark for stable governance and a bitter reminder of how far the state has fallen.

The crowning achievement of the previous administration was its meticulous commitment to preserving constitutional harmony and institutional traditions. Negeri Sembilan’s governance model is uniquely complex, relying on a centuries-old, delicate equilibrium between a modern elected executive, the monarchy, and the state’s sacred, uncodified Adat Perpatih (customary law) institutions.

Aminuddin’s government managed this sensitive balance not by luck, but through sheer political maturity and institutional restraint. Recognising the vital need to insulate daily partisan politics from royal affairs, his government maintained a peaceful, respectful coexistence between elected officials, the Undang Yang Empat (traditional chieftains), and the Yang Dipertuan Besar.
Mutual respect
It was a partnership built on mutual respect and systemic boundaries, ensuring that time-honoured traditions and modern democracy reinforced rather than undermined one another.

Crucially, this political maturity served as a protective shield that insulated the state from systemic crises. Backers of the previous government frequently note that the coalition successfully shielded the civil service and state apparatus from being dragged into protracted constitutional disputes.

Today, we realise just how vital that bulwark was, and how easily it could be dismantled by naked political opportunism. The moment the BN-PH cooperation fractured, it triggered an unprecedented and destructive chain reaction that has shaken the state to its core.

The descent into absolute turmoil accelerated rapidly last April, when 14 BN assemblymen abruptly withdrew their support from Aminuddin’s government following a dispute involving royal affairs. Rather than prioritising state stability, this drastic move plunged the state into a perilous political vacuum, leaving a minority government in its wake and forcing a snap election.

This vacuum did more than just disrupt daily executive governance; it threw open the doors to the current existential crisis— an unprecedented, overt succession dispute between Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir and Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar, who is backed by the current administration.
Constitutional deadlock
The collapse of the foundational political consensus has dragged the state legislative assembly into a complex, multi-layered constitutional deadlock with no clear legal exit ramp.

We are now forced to witness an extraordinary and embarrassing clash of powers. In direct response to aggressive moves by the new state executive council supporting a proclamation to depose him, Tuanku Muhriz took the radical but decisive step of revoking the appointments of all 10 state executive councillors. Citing a direct breach of their oaths of office, the palace purged the state cabinet in one swift stroke.

The fallout has left governance not just shaky, but completely paralysed. The current menteri besar, Ismail Lasim, now stands isolated—a lone captain aboard a ghost ship. In a bizarre attempt to downplay this structural damage, Ismail has chosen to prioritise appointing village chiefs and village development and security committees rather than resolving the critical vacancies in his cabinet.

To claim that state administration is "running smoothly" while the formal sitting of the state assembly has been indefinitely postponed until late November is an insult to the voters' intelligence. This represents a profound failure of the democratic apparatus, where grassroots local appointments are being deployed as a smoke screen to mask a total absence of executive authority.
Painful lesson

Negeri Sembilan is learning a painful lesson first-hand: when you dismantle a functional political consensus for short-term gain, the alternative is rarely better. The current turmoil proves that the previous BN-PH ruling alliance was not merely a marriage of convenience — it was a vital stabilising force.

The current menteri besar cannot continue to govern in a state of absolute paralysis, pretending that village-level appointments can substitute for a functioning state legislative assembly or a complete Exco line-up.

The state’s political leaders must urgently put aside partisan egos, halt their dangerous chess game against traditional institutions, and return to the constitutional blueprint that guaranteed peace for years. The state's executive vacuum is no longer an isolated political squabble; it is a systemic crisis threatening the very fabric of Negeri Sembilan’s unique identity.
If the current leadership is incapable of restoring the stable, respectful equilibrium of the past, they must accept their failure and step aside for those who can.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

5896ab894451fee5: Over the Merdeka holidays, I went fishing with some friends off the Pahang and Johor coast. We started off from the Kuala Rompin jetties on a lovely morning with mist shrouding the mangrove and hovering over the river. It was a beautiful, peaceful sight.

Then the sun started getting hotter but the mist remained… and remained, acting in a most un-misty way. When we sailed away from the river mouth we could still see this “mist” all around us. It wasn’t mist. It was the haze, right there on the east coast hundreds of kilometres from the nearest Indonesian territories, yet enough of it was visible even in Pulau Tioman.

Over the last few months, I've been saying “I've never seen haze this bad, only to update it again multiple times on subsequent days. The haze last week was especially bad, but I’m sure as records go this too will be broken soon.

What can I say about the haze that hasn’t been said by many for years? I’m relatively healthy for my age and don’t have any bad allergy problems, but I still get headaches and nausea because of it. I can’t bear to think about what those with actual health issues must be going through.
The current haze seems worse than previous ones. It hangs heavy and feels thick and foul, often covering the sun and hills and gloomily blocking vision to barely a kilometre or so on the highway.

Everybody is frustrated with it, including an Indonesian official who slammed his Malaysian and Singaporean neighbours for complaining about the haze from Sumatra without acknowledging it also gives us oxygen during better days.

Hello! Our Indonesian official friend forgets his high school chemistry. Sumatra is passing us more than oxygen now, this time the said oxygen is all bound up with carbon and sulphur and nitrogen and other elements to form noxious and poisonous monoxides and dioxides and ozone!
Not exactly the kind of trade among friends. After decades of “importing” this stuff for months most years, we deserve a breather, if you’ll pardon the expression.
The Indonesians are also experimenting with clearing the haze with dry ice, which is supposed to lift the smoke particles higher into the atmosphere and clear the land.

Great – now the smoke particles will go even higher into the Indonesian skies to catch the stronger monsoon wind up there and even more of them can waft their way to Malaysia. Thank you again Indonesia!

In reality, Indonesia’s forest fire problem has gotten out of hand. The fires have literally gone underground, setting off the uncontrollable burning of dry underground peat. Once this catches fire, only the deluge of a monsoon can put it out.

This year a combination of factors, including a more severe El Nino, is exacerbating the problem; perhaps a madder-than-usual rush to burn forests, because there’s less of them left every year, is making things worse.

What we need to see is a more aggressive attitude among the political leaders of the region in fighting this menace. Our own leaders must also start demanding more be done by Indonesia to stop this perennial curse.

Of the culprits setting the forest on fire in Sumatra and Kalimantan are believed to include some big Malaysian plantation companies. If that is so, bring them to account and throw the book at them: I can guarantee there’ll be loud cheers from us ordinary Malaysians.
And ordinary Indonesians too. If it’s bad for us hundreds of kilometres away from the worst of it, just imagine how bad it must be for the unfortunate people living right there.

They can't go fishing away from the haze, like I did. They can’t get into private jets and fly out of the country to foreign clearer skies, as some people did. They just have to stay there and suck it all in literally and suffer now and/or die earlier later.

Our problems are not with the ordinary Indonesians, many of whom suffer even worse than us because of this haze. Our issues are with the Indonesian authorities who we don’t see treating the problem as the emergency it actually is.
And our issue is also with our own leaders who are more interested in maintaining peace and harmony while our people are literally choking with illness and maybe even death.

f767688b52eef969: The U.S. House of Representatives votes on the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022. AP Photo/Patrick SemanskyA massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate. But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it. Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris. It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions, primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient, rather than by imposing new fees or taxes. Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives. While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts. Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects. Benefits of federal investment Elected officials are sometimes accused of “pork barrel politics,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth. Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.” That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them. A Toyota battery-manufacturing plant in Liberty, N.C., received billions in support through the Inflation Reduction Act. Logan Cyrus/AFP via Getty Images The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election. During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “economic development opportunities,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself. Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles. In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022. We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022. When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result. Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have. These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding. While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections, we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas. President Donald Trump signs a major tax cut and spending cut bill on July 4, 2025. Samuel Corum/Getty Images Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions. A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases. The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands. This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership. These electoral benefits indicate voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious. Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines, even if those benefits are not enough to overcome national divisions over climate change. This article is based on research conducted with Nives Dolsak, Inhwan Ko, and Aseem Prakash. 0dbde1ea11534cb3: Despite millions of years of evolution, the development of the human fetus remains a complex process that is vulnerable to genetic, environmental, and metabolic disruptions. These disruptions could result in developmental abnormalities, starting with one of the first organs to begin developing in the fetus that continues to develop after birth: the brain. In a routine prenatal ultrasound, the sonographer will flag possible brain abnormalities for additional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). But imperfect imaging can result in missed or incorrect diagnoses.  To assist with the early detection and treatment of these abnormalities, researchers at MIT, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Inria have developed and trained a deep learning model called E(3)-Pose that helps image the fetus’s head while it’s in motion to capture a high-resolution image that the radiologist can examine. A paper about the work was presented at the 2026 European Conference on Computer Vision.  “One of the problems with having the baby move is that the slices are all over the place,” says first author Ramya Muthukrishnan. Muthukrishnan is an MIT PhD student in the lab of Sunlin (1966) and Priscilla Chou Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Polina Golland, who is a principal investigator at the MIT Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). By slices, Muthukrishnan is referring to a series of 2D images taken during a fetal MRI scan. These 2D planes stacked together effectively make up one high-resolution, 3D image of the fetus’s head. But if the head shifts during imaging, each 2D image “slice” could end up being taken from a different angle, resulting in gaps in the final scan and unusual slice orientation. These problems may cause the physician reviewing the MRI to miss or incorrectly diagnose a pathology in the fetal brain. “There are very fine details that you need a very good volumetric picture of the brain to see,” explains Muthukrishnan. “If you have coverage gaps, you can’t see critical regions, and you need to be able to see well to detect abnormal development.” What makes E(3)-Pose particularly good at tracking fetal motion is its focus on physics. Rather than simply training the model to learn physics from the data, the very principles of physics are baked into the neural network: left-right symmetry of the fetal head is embedded in the model architecture, making it easier for the model to accurately identify the brain’s orientation.  When Muthukrishnan began working on the project at the start of her PhD, she had no background in physics, let alone MRI physics. Most of her experience was in computer science. “I was surprised when I had to go and implement this on the scanner,” she recalls. “I was not prepared for how many times I would crash the scanner because putting things on hardware and getting it to work on hardware is a different beast than training a model to run on data on a GPU.”  Despite the challenges, Muthukrishnan persisted. She remembers shadowing a radiologist who performed fetal MRI scans at Boston Children’s Hospital at the start of her PhD and observing the shared frustration of the patient and radiologist: the pregnant mother felt uncomfortable after spending an hour in an MRI, only to quit the scan halfway; the radiologist was unable to procure a full, high-quality MRI to monitor the development of the fetus. “Seeing frustration about it helped me decide what I wanted to do with my PhD, because it felt like this was a pain point,” Muthukrishnan says. Fortunately, she had help: Co-author Borjan Gagoski, an assistant professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at Boston Children's Hospital, developed a sequence that acquires additional MRI scans to assist with training E(3)-Pose and worked with Muthukrishnan to help troubleshoot the scanner whenever it crashed. Co-author and Boston Children’s Research Assistant Aryn Lee recruited the pregnant volunteers and assisted with acquiring each of the MRI scans. Senior authors who helped guide the project include Elfar Adalsteinsson, MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science; Ellen Grant, the Käthe Beutler Professor of Pediatrics and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School; and Golland. Benjamin Billot, a researcher at Inria and a former postdoc in Golland’s group, helped Muthukrishnan get started with the initial method he developed. “Ramya’s work elegantly combines geometric concepts like equivariance and symmetry with the power of deep learning to change how MRI scanners acquire the images, and to ultimately help the physicians detect and treat problems early in development. It’s an impressive research project that is deep and fundamental in how it models image acquisition, with clear clinical impact,” says Golland. Grant, who directs the Fetal Neonatal Neuroimaging and Developmental Science Center (FNNDSC) at Boston Children’s, adds that Muthukrishnan’s work “will automate fetal brain MRI, replacing today's slow, manual process with faster and more comfortable scans for mothers, while also providing higher-quality images for radiologists to interpret.” E(3)-Pose’s applications could extend beyond motion tracking for fetal MRIs. It could assist with imaging other hard-to-image anatomy, and even autonomous driving applications, where limited sensors need to capture noisy, 3D data in order to track 3D objects. For now, Muthukrishnan hopes to improve E(3)-Pose so that it can help with imaging second-trimester or younger fetuses, as the model is primarily trained on third trimester fetuses. Second-trimester fetuses are “so small, they move around a lot more because there’s more space in the uterus,” Muthukrishnan says. “They’re more important to focus on because the earlier you detect brain abnormalities, the easier it is to intervene.”  This work is supported by the MIT Jameel Clinic, the MIT Takeda Program, the Chou Family Transformative Research Fund, the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering, and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.
1375bb961f6a8369: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games, with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms. Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely.

Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflux, which had been set to go live with today's launch of Steam Next Fest.

In a post on social media Friday evening, the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, "we're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch."
